heading: INT. ASHWORTH HOUSE - GLASS CONSERVATORY - DAY (1887)

units.text: INT. ASHWORTH HOUSE - GLASS CONSERVATORY - DAY (1887)
Ferns crowd the brick walls, and a wrought-iron table holds a gas lamp, an inkwell, and a half-written letter.
PRUDENCE ASHWORTH, 30s, in a gray morning dress with ink on her second finger, sits with a pen poised.
She dips the nib, hesitates, and sets it down again.
She picks up the letter and reads it to the empty air.
My dear Edmund. The orchids you left have bloomed, the white ones, as you said they would. I did not water them as you instructed. I let the rain do it.
units.name: PRUDENCE

units.text: She smooths the page, gazes at a fern, and turns back to the page.
Mrs. Pell asks whether you will be home for the Harvest supper. I told her I did not know. That is the truth. I know very little these days, except the names of plants.
units.name: PRUDENCE

units.text: A drop of water falls from a cracked pane onto the paper.
It spreads and blurs the word "plants."
She lifts the pen, holds it over the page for a long moment, and then, very gently, puts it down in the inkwell and leaves the letter unsigned.
